design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects pairwise meta-analyses (PROSPERO CRD42022355572) of side effects of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in phase 2 and 3 studies across psychiatric indications, searched to 30 October 2023 in PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, MEDLINE and CENTRAL. 13 studies (333 unique participants) in the review, 8 randomized trials (298 participants) in the meta-analyses, analysed separately for phase 2 (spontaneously reported expected reactions and treatment-emergent adverse events) and phase 3 (treatment-emergent adverse events and adverse events of special interest). Also assessed the reporting of harms against CONSORT Harms 2022 and compared adverse-event counts in publications with those in ClinicalTrials.gov. Independent academic review (University of Melbourne), funded by the Australian Medical Research Future Fund.
can_establish: Which side effects were reported more often with MDMA than with placebo or low-dose MDMA in the published trials up to October 2023, how complete and standardized the reporting of harms was, and how many registered adverse events were missing from the publications.
cannot_establish: Rates of side effects per person (the unit of the pooled 'any side effect' outcomes is unclear), rare or delayed harms (studies small and short, most data from PTSD trials of one sponsor), or harms outside the trials' screened populations.

sample.recruitment: Database search from inception to 30 October 2023 (search re-run just before the final analysis), English-language peer-reviewed articles of MDMA given with psychotherapy for a psychiatric condition; phase 1 studies without psychotherapy excluded (Methods › Search strategy; Inclusion and exclusion criteria).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: one or more MDMA doses combined with psychotherapy to treat a target psychiatric condition, any design. Excluded: studies without psychotherapy, papers without original data, conference abstracts, book chapters, animal studies.
sample.demographics: Table 1, by study: PTSD in 10 of 13 studies (8 PTSD trials or open studies plus the long-term follow-up and the couples study with one partner with PTSD), autistic adults with social anxiety (Danforth 2018, 12), alcohol use disorder (Sessa 2021, open-label, 14), and a Swiss case series with various treatment-resistant disorders (Oehen & Gasser 2022, 50, of whom 6 received MDMA only). Ages 31 to 48 on average; percentage female from 17 to 100.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; withdrawal for any reason was analysed as an outcome.
sample.selection_effects: Restrictive search string (MDMA AND psychotherapy or therapy AND 'safe' or 'side' or 'adverse', without truncation shown), English and peer-reviewed only, no search of trial registries for studies. The randomized trial in anxiety with a life-threatening illness (Wolfson et al., 2020), cited in the review's introduction, is not among the included studies. The evidence is mostly from trials funded by one sponsor (MAPS), as the authors note.

exposure.measurement: MDMA-assisted psychotherapy as delivered in each study (Table 1): one to three MDMA sessions with preparatory and integration psychotherapy; doses in the MDMA groups were pooled.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed in Table 1: oral MDMA from 50 mg (Bouso 2008, one session) to 125 to 150 mg (Oehen 2013), with optional supplemental half doses in most trials; phase 3 trials 80 mg in the first session and 120 mg in later ones plus optional half doses.
exposure.polysubstance: Prior MDMA or ecstasy use was extracted: from 0% (Bouso; Danforth) to 51.0% lifetime (MAPP2 placebo arm); not reported in several studies (Table 1).

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo (Bouso, Danforth, Mitchell 2021 and 2023, Mithoefer 2011) or low-dose MDMA as active placebo (25 mg Oehen 2013, 30 mg Mithoefer 2018, 40 mg Ot'alora 2018), pooled together as 'control' (Methods › Data synthesis, 2nd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Side effects as each study defined them: in phase 2, 'spontaneously reported reactions' from a list of reactions expected from healthy-volunteer studies, during sessions and for 7 days after, and treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs: events not on the list or lasting more than 7 days), including psychiatric TEAEs; in phase 3, TEAEs over the whole treatment period and adverse events of special interest (cardiac, suicidality, abuse, misuse or diversion). Withdrawal for any reason. Reporting quality: 17-item CONSORT Harms 2022 checklist, adequate if 70% or more.
outcomes.validity_norms: Most studies relied on passive monitoring of spontaneous reports (11 of 13); one used the UKU side-effect scale (Bouso); eight used the C-SSRS for suicidality (Results › Systematic review: measurement of side effects).
outcomes.operationalization: Odds of experiencing an outcome with MDMA against control, Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 64 outcomes meta-analysed at p < 0.05, of which the significant ones are shown in Fig. 2 and the rest in Supplementary Table 3 (not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Screening of titles and abstracts by one reviewer; full texts by two independent reviewers; extraction by one reviewer checked by a second; RoB 2 and CONSORT Harms scoring by two reviewers independently; GRADE by two reviewers.

analysis.effect_sizes: Phase 2: any side effect during medication sessions OR 1.67 (95% CI 1.12 to 2.49), p = 0.01, 45% against 30%; in the 7 days after OR 1.59 (1.12 to 2.24), p = 0.007, 46% against 31%; anxiety OR 4.7 and jaw clenching OR 4.8 during sessions (intervals in Fig. 2, an image, not extracted); in PTSD studies anxiety OR 4.1 during sessions and 4.8 in the 7 days after; no difference in TEAEs or psychiatric TEAEs, except lower odds of any TEAE with MDMA in the PTSD subgroup (OR 0.5, two studies with low-dose controls). Phase 3: any TEAE OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46), p < 0.001, 16% against 5%; 13 specific TEAEs more likely; no difference in suicidality or cardiac adverse events of special interest; none for abuse, misuse or diversion. Withdrawal: no difference. Heterogeneity described as low; I2 values are in Fig. 2 and the supplement (not extracted).
analysis.covariates: Subgroup analyses of PTSD against non-PTSD studies; sensitivity analyses by method of side-effect assessment and number of medication sessions, which did not change the results.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42022355572; PRISMA reporting. The article does not say whether any analysis departed from the protocol (protocol not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only primary outcomes and significant secondary outcomes are reported in the text and Fig. 2; the other secondary outcomes are in Supplementary Table 3 (not read).
analysis.power: Publication bias not assessed (10 or fewer studies per analysis); the authors note that rare events such as cardiac or suicidality events were unlikely to reach significance.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In mostly PTSD trials, mostly funded by one sponsor, MDMA was associated with more frequent expected side effects during and in the week after sessions (phase 2) and with more treatment-emergent adverse events of 13 named kinds over treatment (phase 3), without differences in psychiatric TEAEs, suicidality or cardiac events of special interest, or withdrawal; certainty very low to moderate; seven of eight trials at high risk of bias; no trial reported harms adequately; more than half the registered non-serious adverse events and 4 of 13 serious adverse events were missing from the publications.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusion say side effects were largely transient and mild or moderate, and the authors call for caution, independent trials and post-marketing studies. The severity and transience statements rest on how the primary trials described their events; the review itself graded no severity data. Calling the review comprehensive and 'across indications' overstates its reach: one randomized trial outside PTSD was included, and one known randomized trial outside PTSD was not.

timeline.event: Breeksema et al. systematic review of adverse events with psychedelics and MDMA (no meta-analysis) finds mostly transient acute and late adverse events and poor assessment of harms.
Kisely et al. meta-analysis of psilocybin and MDMA trials, cited by this review as an earlier meta-analysis of side effects (not read here).
This review (published online 23 April 2024), before the August 2024 retraction of two analyses it cites (Jerome et al., 2020, and Mithoefer et al., 2019).
Commentary on this review in the same journal (Murray, 2024; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of MDMA-assisted therapy side effects across indications found here. Its direction agrees with the phase 3 trial reports read by the project (sc_mitchell_2021, sc_mitchell_2023) and with Breeksema et al. (2022), but it pools mostly the same sponsor's trials; its 'any side effect' estimates are of uncertain unit; and its registry comparison is the most useful original contribution.

funding.funder: Medical Research Future Fund of Australia (MRF2010957); open access funded by CAUL.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Melbourne (Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences; Centre for Youth Mental Health and Orygen). None of the authors ran the included trials.

what_would_settle_it: Independent trials outside PTSD and outside one sponsor's programme that assess side effects systematically (structured checklists at fixed times, including between sessions and at long-term follow-up), report all events by arm with denominators, and register them; and an individual-participant-data meta-analysis with the participant as unit of analysis.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (psychiatric conditions), intervention (MDMA with psychotherapy), comparator (control) and outcomes (side effects, withdrawal) are stated.
PROSPERO CRD42022355572; the article does not report whether the analyses followed the protocol or justify any deviation.
All designs combining MDMA with psychotherapy, with the reason phase 1 studies are excluded.

Five databases, but English-language and peer-reviewed articles only without justification, a narrow search string, no registry, grey-literature or reference-list searching for studies, and an eligible randomized trial (Wolfson et al., 2020) that the review cites but does not include.
Titles and abstracts screened by one reviewer; only full texts by two.
Extraction by one reviewer checked for accuracy and completeness by a second.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the article lists only the five studies excluded from the meta-analyses (Table S2) and shows the flow in Fig. 1 (an image); whether the supplement lists the excluded full texts with reasons could not be checked (supplement not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives population, doses, controls, prior MDMA use and how side effects were assessed and reported; settings and follow-up periods are given only partly.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 in duplicate for the eight randomized trials (kappa 1.00); the five non-randomized studies in the review were not appraised for risk of bias.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported for the included studies, although the authors note that most were sponsored by one advocacy group.

Random-effects Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios, but the unit of analysis of the 'any side effect' outcomes is not stated and cannot be the participant (16% with any TEAE on MDMA in phase 3, while 58.5 to 63% had muscle tightness alone); event counts per session and participant counts appear side by side in Table 1; placebo and low-dose MDMA controls are pooled.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Seven of eight trials at high risk; no analysis of the effect of risk of bias on the estimates (sensitivity analyses concern assessment method and number of sessions).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The authors stress high risk of bias and very low to moderate certainty and ask for cautious interpretation.
Heterogeneity reported as low; phase 2 and 3 analysed separately because of different reporting; PTSD subgroups; the active-control issue discussed.
Not assessed because 10 or fewer studies per analysis; possible sources (small studies from one advocacy sponsor) are mentioned but not investigated.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and the absence of competing interests are stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence when more than one critical item fails: here the search (4), the statistical methods (11) and publication bias (15); item 7 is provisional (supplement not read) but cannot change the rating. This judges the pooled numbers as unbiased summaries, not the review's usefulness: its registry comparison, its CONSORT Harms audit and its tabulation of the trials' side-effect data are valuable and are what claims should cite, with the pooled odds ratios as indicating direction only.

key_findings.finding: 13 studies with 333 unique participants met the criteria; 5 without a control group were excluded from the meta-analyses; the remaining 8 randomized trials (298 participants) reported 138 safety outcomes, of which 64 had data from at least two studies.

Included studies (Table 1): randomized trials in PTSD (Bouso 2008, 6; Mithoefer 2011, 20; Oehen 2013, 12; Mithoefer 2018, 26; Ot'alora 2018, 28; Mitchell 2021, 90; Mitchell 2023, 104) and in autistic adults with social anxiety (Danforth 2018, 12); non-randomized: an open-label PTSD study (Jardim 2021, 3), a pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials (Jerome 2020, 107), an uncontrolled couples study with one partner with PTSD (Monson 2020, 12), a Swiss case series of various treatment-resistant disorders (Oehen & Gasser 2022, 50) and an open-label alcohol use disorder study (Sessa 2021, 14).
key_findings.note: Jerome et al. (2020) was retracted in August 2024; its rows must not be cited. The randomized trial in anxiety with a life-threatening illness (Wolfson et al., 2020) is cited in the Introduction but not included.

key_findings.finding: Phase 2 trials: any side effect during medication sessions OR 1.67 (95% CI 1.12 to 2.49), 45% against 30%; in the 7 days after OR 1.59 (1.12 to 2.24), 46% against 31%; anxiety (OR 4.7) and jaw clenching (OR 4.8) during sessions more likely with MDMA; in PTSD studies anxiety OR 4.1 during sessions and 4.8 in the following 7 days.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › Phase two studies, side effects during and 7 days following medication sessions; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 2 legend
key_findings.note: The percentages cannot be shares of participants with any side effect (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Phase 2 trials: no difference in any treatment-emergent adverse event or psychiatric TEAE; in PTSD studies only, lower odds of any TEAE with MDMA (OR 0.5), from two studies whose controls were low-dose MDMA.
key_findings.locator: Results › Phase two studies › Treatment emergent adverse events, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Phase 3 trials (194 participants): any TEAE OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46), 16% against 5%; more likely with MDMA: muscle tightness, decreased appetite, nausea, excessive perspiration, feeling cold, restlessness, dilated pupils, jaw clenching or tight jaw, uncontrolled eye movements, feeling jittery, non-cardiac chest pain or discomfort, blurred vision and chills.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › Phase three studies › Treatment emergent adverse events, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Phase 3: no difference in adverse events of special interest for suicidality or cardiac function; no AESIs for MDMA abuse, misuse or diversion reported. Withdrawal for any reason: no difference across all studies or in PTSD studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Phase three studies › Adverse event of special interest; Phase 2 and 3 studies › Withdrawal

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (RoB 2, outcome side effects): 7 of the 8 meta-analysed trials high, 1 some concerns (Danforth 2018); measurement of the outcome the domain most often high; kappa 1.00. GRADE: very low for all phase 2 primary outcomes, low for two and moderate for one phase 3 primary outcome, moderate for withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › Certainty of evidence

key_findings.finding: No trial adhered adequately (70% or more) to CONSORT Harms 2022; median adherence 50% (range 21% to 64%); no trial reported effect sizes with precision for harms or absolute and relative effects.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adherence to CONSORT Harms 2022; Table 2

key_findings.finding: ClinicalTrials.gov against publications: 1487 non-serious adverse events in the registers against 661 in the articles (5 trials comparable) and 13 serious adverse events against 9 (8 trials); the 4 unpublished serious events were all in MDMA groups (metastases to the central nervous system, clavicle fracture, syncope, suicidal behaviour). 56% of non-serious and 31% of serious registered events were not in the articles; the phase 3 reports listed only events with at least a twofold difference between arms.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of adverse events published versus reported on ClinicalTrial.gov; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Measurement: 11 of 13 studies relied on passive monitoring of spontaneous reports; one used a structured side-effect scale (UKU, Bouso 2008); eight used the C-SSRS. Phase 2 trials collected expected reactions separately from TEAEs; phase 3 trials reported only TEAEs over the treatment period.
key_findings.locator: Results › Systematic review: measurement of side effects; Systematic review: reporting of side effects

key_findings.finding: Authors' limits: conclusions only for acute and short-term side effects, insufficient data on longer-term risks; highly selective samples; small studies sponsored largely by a single advocacy group; implementation outside trials likely to increase side effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The proportions given for 'any' side effect cannot be shares of participants: in phase 3, 16% of MDMA participants are said to have had a TEAE, while Table 1 lists muscle tightness alone in 63% (Mitchell 2021) and 58.5% (Mitchell 2023) of MDMA participants; in phase 2, 45% with any side effect during sessions, while Table 1 lists anxiety during MDMA sessions in 59% to 89% of MDMA participants in individual trials. The unit of analysis is not stated; with 194 phase 3 participants, the narrow interval for OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46) also suggests that events or participant-by-event entries were counted.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Phase two studies; Results › Phase three studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1)
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled 'any side effect' odds ratios cannot be read as odds per person and their intervals are probably too narrow; claims should cite them for direction only, and use trial-level percentages for frequencies.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 reports some studies' side effects as numbers of events and percentages of sessions (Jardim 2021, Mithoefer 2011, Oehen 2013, Monson 2020) and others as participants; the Methods do not say how these were combined in the meta-analyses.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1; Methods › Data synthesis, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Adds to the uncertainty about the unit of analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: Wolfson et al. (2020), a randomized trial of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for anxiety with a life-threatening illness, is cited in the Introduction (reference 7) as evidence of potential in other conditions, but is not among the 13 included studies, and no reason is given in the article.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Introduction, 1st paragraph; Table 1; reference list)
reporting_issues.consequence: The review is not complete for indications other than PTSD; non-PTSD randomized data rest on one trial of 12 people.

reporting_issues.issue: Two sources since retracted are used: the pooled long-term follow-up by Jerome et al. (2020) is an included study (Table 1, the review's only long-term harm data, including 9.6% using ecstasy or MDMA after treatment), and the phase 2 outcome categories are defined with reference to Mithoefer et al. (2019). Both were retracted in August 2024, after this review was published; PMC now marks them.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1; Methods › Data synthesis, 3rd paragraph; references 28 and 44)
reporting_issues.consequence: The long-term harm data in Table 1 must not be cited; the meta-analyses are unaffected because the follow-up had no control group.

reporting_issues.issue: Bouso et al. is dated 2008 in Table 1 and the reference list but 2011 in the header of Table 2.
